destination.title: He Drove Home Honking. The Police Followed Him Inside.

short14: An officer chases you over something minor, and you step inside your home.
One man was just playing his music too loud.
An officer flipped on his lights, and the man pulled into his own garage.
The officer stuck his foot under the closing garage door, and walked right in.
In 2021, the Supreme Court said no: chasing a minor offense, by itself, does not automatically let police enter your home.
They need a warrant, or a real emergency.
Your home is still the hardest place for the state to enter.
Watch the full story on the channel.

candidate_payload_lines: The officer walks up and sticks his foot under the descending door, stopping it, and steps inside — no warrant, no permission .
In 2021, the Supreme Court took up exactly this question, and the answer is one of the clearest statements in years about the one place the law still treats as a fortress: your home .
As a rule, the police cannot enter your home without a warrant — that is the baseline, and the exceptions to it are narrow .

The question the courts had to answer is the one step before that: was the officer allowed to enter the garage at all — to follow a man into his home over a minor offense, without a warrant — just because that man had not pulled over?
If a dangerous suspect runs into a house, no one thinks the police must stop politely at the door and go find a judge .
In 2021, the Supreme Court rejected the automatic rule.

lines.text: People hear that the Supreme Court stopped police following you into your home. That is not quite what happened.
source_lines: In 2021, the Supreme Court rejected the automatic rule.

lines.text: What the Court rejected in 2021 was the automatic rule. Chasing someone over a minor offence does not, by itself, open your door.
source_lines: In 2021, the Supreme Court rejected the automatic rule.

lines.text: Because if a dangerous suspect runs into a house, nobody thinks the police must stop politely at the door and go find a judge.
source_lines: If a dangerous suspect runs into a house, no one thinks the police must stop politely at the door and go find a judge.

lines.text: So the answer is not never. The answer is: not automatically, and not for anything.
source_lines: In 2021, the Supreme Court rejected the automatic rule.

lines.text: A misdemeanor can mean a violent assault. It can also mean jaywalking, an open container, or a complaint about music played too loud.
source_lines: And the range of "misdemeanor" really is enormous.
It can mean a violent assault — or it can mean jaywalking, an open container, a noise complaint, playing your music too loud.

lines.text: Justice Kagan wrote that flight is a fact an officer can weigh, but the emergency is not there every time. Someone has to look.
source_lines: The principal opinion was written by Justice Elena Kagan.
Flight, she explained, is a real and relevant fact — an officer can absolutely consider it.
The point is that you have to actually look.

lines.text: All nine justices agreed on the result, but not on the reasoning. Roberts and Alito wanted a broader rule that would let officers in.
source_lines: The result was unanimous — all nine justices agreed to send the case back.
Chief Justice John Roberts, joined by Justice Samuel Alito, wrote separately.

They agreed with the outcome here, but they argued for a broader rule: that hot pursuit of a fleeing suspect should generally justify entry, because an officer in a chase cannot safely pause to weigh the seriousness of the offense, and because letting suspects escape into their homes invites exactly that.

lines.text: Case by case. Every single time. Which is why this one keeps being repeated as something it never actually said.

shorts.angle: The baseline nobody states out loud: without a warrant, your door stays shut.
shorts.type: A — the rule the exceptions hang off
shorts.avoids: short14 is about the garage and the 2021 ruling. It never states the underlying baseline or how narrow the exceptions are.
shorts.funnel_question_left_for_longform: How narrow is narrow — what actually counts as an emergency?
shorts.loop_join: L5 points back to where the rule starts, and L1 is that starting point, the baseline everyone skips.

lines.text: Start from the rule everyone skips. As a baseline, police cannot enter your home without a warrant.
source_lines: As a rule, the police cannot enter your home without a warrant — that is the baseline, and the exceptions to it are narrow.

lines.text: The exceptions to that are narrow. Narrow is doing a lot of work in that sentence.
source_lines: As a rule, the police cannot enter your home without a warrant — that is the baseline, and the exceptions to it are narrow.

lines.text: One night an officer put his foot under a descending garage door, stopped it, and stepped inside. No warrant. No permission.
source_lines: The officer walks up and sticks his foot under the descending door, stopping it, and steps inside — no warrant, no permission.

lines.text: The question was not whether the man was guilty of anything. It was whether the officer was allowed through that door at all.
source_lines: The question the courts had to answer is the one step before that: was the officer allowed to enter the garage at all

lines.text: One of those exceptions is an emergency the law calls exigent circumstances: evidence about to be destroyed, a person in danger, a suspect escaping.
source_lines: One of those exceptions is an emergency the law calls "exigent circumstances," and a classic example is hot pursuit: an officer chasing a fleeing suspect.
They cover things like someone about to destroy evidence, a person in danger, or a suspect actively escaping.

lines.text: California argued the answer was yes, automatically. Any flight, even from a misdemeanor, would count as the emergency. Flight in, door open.
source_lines: California's answer was yes, automatically.
Under the rule the state defended, whenever a suspect flees — even from a misdemeanor — that flight by itself creates the kind of emergency that lets police enter a home in pursuit.
No case-by-case judgment required.

lines.text: If any flight from any offense opened the door, the strongest protection in the Fourth Amendment could be switched off by a trivial chase.
source_lines: On the other side: the home cannot lose its constitutional protection over a honking horn.
If any flight, from any offense, automatically opens your door to the police, then the strongest protection in the Fourth Amendment can be switched off by the most trivial chase.

lines.text: In 2021 the Supreme Court answered it. And the answer only makes sense if you know where the whole thing begins.
